newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac slams racial hate in speech to French Jews.
newsitem.headline: Chirac slams racial hate in speech to French Jews.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac reached out to Jewish voters on Sunday with praise for cultural integration in France and a denunciation of racial hatred.
But the Gaullist head of state, in a speech to Jewish leaders at the Paris city hall, also reaffirmed his strong backing for a government drive to clamp down on illegal immigration.
And he disappointed his audience by failing to address criticisms that he was biased against Israel in the quest for a Middle East peace.

Some Jewish leaders had predicted Chirac would use the speech, billed in advance as a major address, to make a gesture of reconciliation after angering Israeli officials and French Jews during a recent visit to Jerusalem.

During the visit, Chirac publicly argued with Israeli security guards in Jerusalem's Old City and repeatedly called for a Palestinian state and the exchange of land for peace in occupied Arab lands -- policies opposed by hard-line Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Chirac never brought up the Middle East in his speech, which was delivered at a ceremony marking the 190th anniversary of Napoleon's recognition of religious freedom for French Jews.
Instead he warned of the dangers of illegal immigration while praising cultural integration and denouncing racism.
"We must reaffirm our commitment to integration, which is best accomplished by a strong stand against illegal immigration," Chirac said.

"Nothing would be more dangerous for the foreigners living legally in France and their children who have a calling to be French...than a lax and ambiguous stance that would soon feed the forces of hate," he said.

"The France which we love, and which we want, is not and will never be a mosaic of different communities juxtaposed on one another. Ours is an open nation, generous but inflexible on its fundamental values," Chirac said.

Artists, intellectuals and leftist politicians this month accused Chirac's centre-right government of pandering to the far-right National Front and fostering racism and xenophobia in battling fiercely in parliament for a bill to tighten already tough laws against illegal immigration.
The bill passed the National Assembly last week and is due for a final reading in the Senate beginning on March 11.
Le Pen took credit for the government initiative even as he criticised it for being too weak.
In a book to be published this week, Le Pen is quoted accusing the president of being hostile to the National Front because he was in the pay of Jewish organisations.

According to the book, Le Pen said Jewish organisations had barred Chirac from denouncing Communism and that Chirac had made a commitment to the B'nai Brith and "other foreign societies" never to form an alliance with the National Front.
Chirac did not mention Le Pen's statements but aides said he had them in mind when he denounced "those who exploit uncertainty about the future...promote fear and stir up hate".

The Jewish leaders applauded just once during his remarks, when he mentioned that he had in July 1995 recognised the responsibility of the collaborationist Vichy regime in the persecution of French Jews during the years of Nazi occupation.
